Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Recognize manifestations of diabetes mellitus in the foot.
Identify indications for the surgical management of manifestations of diabetes mellitus in the
foot.
Stratify the risk of compilations from surgical treatment in a patient with diabetes mellitus.
Review the expected outcomes of surgical procedures for the management of diabetic foot
problems.
Review the following procedures: plantar fascia release, sesamoid shave/excision,
hammer/claw toe correction, first ray dorsiflexion osteotomy, Achilles tendon lengthening,
gastrocnemius recession, Keller procedure, toe amputation, transmetatarsal amputation,
midfoot amputation, hindfoot amputation, and partial calcanectomy.
Overview and Epidemiology

Ulcerations are responsible for 85% of lower extremity amputations and represent the most
common medical complication for which patients with diabetes mellitus seek treatment.1
More than 80,000 diabetes-related amputations of the lower extremity are performed in the
United States each year.1
Medical and surgical advances and improvements in orthotic and prosthetic devices help
many of these patients achieve functional and ambulatory levels similar to preoperative levels.
Approximately 30% of amputees undergo amputation of the contralateral limb within 3 years;
however, the 5-year mortality rate after the amputation of a leg is approximately 66%.1
Indications
Recurrent ulcerations or pre-ulcerative calluses despite nonsurgical management
Ulcers not showing signs of healing after 4 weeks of appropriate management
Osteomyelitis
Necrotic tissue without revascularization options

Indications
Patients who have diabetes mellitus commonly present with foot deformities that
endanger the integrity of the soft-tissue envelope. The combination of neuropathy and
peripheral vascular disease renders the soft tissue especially vulnerable to increased
pressure. Neuropathy interferes with the patient’s ability to perceive the discomfort
caused by avascular tissue. Normal weight bearing results in areas of avascular tissue
that the intact host will offload before tissue damage occurs. Without sensation, the
neuropathic patient fails to offload avascular tissue and necrosis occurs. Neuropathy
also impairs the ability of the intrinsic muscles of the foot to maintain the alignment of
the toes. Toe deformity leads to areas of increased pressure and the development of
pre-ulcerative calluses. Glycosylation of the Achilles tendon results in equinus
contracture, increasing pressure on the forefoot. These processes cause pressure points
that initially result in callus and, eventually, soft-tissue breakdown.
Initial management with appropriate shoes may reduce the need for surgical
management. Calluses may indicate areas of high pressure and may proceed to the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:32 AM
AAOS | Surgical Management of the Diabetic Foot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000551
2/27

development of a diabetic ulcer. Painful calluses should be evaluated for surgical
decompression if nonsurgical management techniques are ineffective. Patients with
recurrent breakdown or ulcerations that do not heal via nonsurgical treatment, such as
total contact cast, are candidates for surgical treatment. (Resource 1; Video 1). Ulcers
that do not improve after 4 weeks of management should be evaluated for surgical
treatment options to reduce the pressure that is preventing healing.
Video 1 Toolan BC, Pinzur MS: Total Contact Casting [video]. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2012. https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-
page/1657__Videos. Accessed March 19, 2021.
Patients may present with infections or necrotic tissues that endanger the foot.
Infections that are causing systemic illness should be urgently débrided and any fluid
collections should be drained. Necrotic tissue should be removed. The viability of the
limb can then be evaluated. Amputations may reduce the systemic burden of an
infection and return a patient to activity more rapidly than medical treatment alone. In
general, amputations are performed at the most distal viable level because of increased
metabolic demand for ambulation at higher levels of amputation.
Contraindications
Peripheral vascular disease
Active infection at the site of the procedure

Malnourished patient
Inability to obtain a prosthesis
Uncontrolled blood glucose level with elevated HgA1C level

Contraindications
The level of surgery often is driven by the presence of peripheral vascular disease. Toe
pressures higher than 30 mm Hg and/or transcutaneous oxygen levels of 25 mm Hg are
good signs for healing after a surgical procedure.2 Erythema and swelling in a limb may
result in values that are artificially low, and these values are not adequate alone to
determine the level of the amputation. The ankle-brachial index often is artificially high
because of arteriosclerosis. If vascular screening tests indicate poor circulation, arterial
Doppler or CT angiography can help determine if a constriction is present that can be
addressed by vascular surgeons.
Osteomyelitis or soft-tissue infection may compromise the results of a corrective
procedure. If the affected tissue is not being removed during the procedure, the
infection should be controlled before the reconstructive procedure. MRI, nuclear
medicine, and positron-emission tomography may aid in determining if infection if
present at the surgical site.
Metabolic studies are useful to determine if a patient is optimized for healing after a
surgical procedure. Many patients with diabetes mellitus will be malnourished. An
albumen level of 30 g/dL and a white blood cell count of 1.5 × 109 cells/L are indicators of
adequate reserves for healing.2 If possible, surgical procedures should be delayed until
the patient is medically optimized to minimize surgical complications.
If the procedure will result in the need for a prosthesis, the patient should be counseled
on prosthesis availability, which may vary based on funding sources. Some amputation
levels may result in considerable disability without an appropriate prosthesis, and soft-
tissue coverage at the amputation site may be at risk of breakdown without the support
of a well-fitted prosthesis (Resource 2).

Techniques
Plantar Fascia Release
Addresses plantar ulcers of the toes and the metatarsophalangeal joint
Indicated for toes with 5° to 30° of dorsiflexion preoperatively
Metatarsophalangeal joint destruction is a contraindication.

Plantar Fascia Release
Limitations in ankle and/or toe dorsiflexion cause an increase in pressure on the plantar
forefoot. This increased pressure may lead to diabetic ulcers that can necessitate
amputations. Reducing pressure on the plantar foot improves healing of forefoot
lesions. If an ulceration is present on the plantar aspect of the toe or the
metatarsophalangeal joint, release of the plantar fascia to that digit may result in
increased range of motion and decreased pressure on the digit. If a severe toe
contracture is present, less than 5° of dorsiflexion is present, or deformity of the toe is
causing increased pressure, alternative procedures are required. The goal of the
procedure is to increase range of motion at least 12°. If destruction of the
metatarsophalangeal joint is present that will prevent this increased range of motion,
plantar fascia release is not effective.3
The procedure is performed under a local anesthetic agent. At the level of the Lisfranc
joint, the individual bands of the plantar fascia can be palpated. The affected toe is
placed in maximum dorsiflexion. A No. 11 scalpel is used to transect the plantar fascia
band to the toe. The surgeon should feel an immediate increase in range of motion of
the toe. The wound is closed with the use of a horizontal mattress suture. The foot is
dressed with a compression dressing, and weight bearing is permitted in a stiff
postoperative shoe. Any ulcer is managed via routine wound care. Range of motion of
the toe is initiated 1 week after the procedure. Patients can return to usual shoe wear
after the wound has healed.
Release of the plantar fascia of a single toe that results in more than a 12° increase of
motion is associated with a 67% healing rate 6 weeks after the procedure. For patients
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:32 AM
AAOS | Surgical Management of the Diabetic Foot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000551
5/27

who do not heal, subsequent Achilles tendon lengthening benefits 40% of patients.
Plantar fascia release is less invasive, associated with a lower complication rate, and
results in faster recovery than Achilles tendon release. Plantar fascia release is a
reasonable consideration for patients with single-digit plantar ulceration and limited
range of motion compared with the other digits.
Sesamoid Shave/Excision
Sesamoids present high-pressure points on the plantar foot.
Partial or complete excision reduces pressure on the underlying ulcer.
Complete excision of both sesamoids is contraindicated.

Sesamoid Shave/Excision
Ulceration under the first metatarsophalangeal joint is common and, because of the high
pressure in this location, may be associated with difficult healing. The tibial sesamoid is
more commonly associated with ulceration. Pressure in this location can be managed via
partial or complete sesamoid excision, dorsiflexion osteotomy of the first ray, resection
of the metatarsal head, or Achilles tendon lengthening.4
Partial medial sesamoid excision is performed through a medial longitudinal incision just
plantar to the midline of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. The plantar sensory nerve
must be identified and protected. The periosteum of the sesamoid is incised, taking care
to avoid entering the metatarsophalangeal joint. A saw is used to resect the plantar half
of the sesamoid, and the edges are smoothed with the use of a rasp. The incision is
closed in a layered manner. The patient is permitted to bear weight in a stiff
postoperative shoe until the wound has healed. Routine wound care for the ulcer is re-
initiated.
Complete sesamoid excision is performed via the same medial approach; however, the
periosteal incision is along the dorsal edge of the flexor hallucis brevis tendon. The flexor
hallucis longus tendon is visualized during resection and must be protected. The
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:32 AM
AAOS | Surgical Management of the Diabetic Foot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000551
6/27

intersesamoid ligament is then sutured to the abductor hallucis longus. The defect is
closed as much as possible. The incision is closed in a layered fashion. Strap, spacer, or
cast immobilization is used to prevent hallux valgus. Forefoot–weight bearing is
restricted for 6 weeks postoperatively. Regular shoe wear is permitted after 12 weeks
postoperatively if wounds have healed. (Figure 1).
Complete resection of both sesamoids is contraindicated because of the risk of complete
dislocation of the first proximal phalanx dorsal. The dorsal dislocated toe will be pressed
on by shoes, resulting in increased pressure under the first metatarsal head. This will
disrupt healing of the ulcer for which the procedure was performed.
Figure 1

Hammer/Claw Toe Correction
Ulceration of the tip of the toe or at the proximal interphalangeal joint that cannot be
addressed via shoe modifications can be managed via deformity correction.
Flexible hammer toes can be corrected via tenotomy.
Rigid hammer toes are managed via resection of the joint.

Hammer/Claw Toe Correction
Toe deformity may increase pressure at the tip of the toe, dorsal proximal
interphalangeal joint, and plantar metatarsal head. Most deformities can be managed
via shoes with a wide toe box and accommodative inserts. Metatarsal pads can be added
to offload the metatarsal heads. If ulcers fail to heal or recur despite shoe modifications,
surgical management is indicated.4
For flexible deformities that can be passively corrected, percutaneous flexor tenotomy
often is effective. This is especially true for ulcerations on the tip of the toe. (Figure 2).
This procedure can be performed in the clinic. The toe is numbed with the use of a local
anesthetic agent. A corrective force is placed on the toe. A No. 15 blade is used to
percutaneously release the tendon at the level of the distal interphalangeal joint. The toe
should be felt to correct with the release. The incision is closed with the use of a simple
suture. Patients are permitted to bear weight in a regular shoe immediately after the
procedure. Wounds may take an extended time to heal.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:32 AM
AAOS | Surgical Management of the Diabetic Foot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000551
8/27

Figure 2
Clinical photograph of a foot with claw toe shows a callus on the tip of the toe (arrow).
(Courtesy of Jerry S. Grimes, MD, Lubbock, TX.)
If the deformity is rigid or pressure is the result of bone prominence at the proximal
interphalangeal joint, resection arthroplasty/fusion of the deformed joint is indicated.
The procedure often can be accomplished under a local anesthetic agent. The approach
involves a full-thickness incision directly over the affected joint. Subperiosteal dissection
frees the collateral ligaments. The more proximal joint surface is excised with the use of
a bone cutter, removing the condyles. The toe is reduced and fixed under fluoroscopic
guidance (Figure 3). Fixation can be either internal implants or wires that protrude from
the tip of the toe. The patient is permitted to bear weight in a rigid shoe. The protruding
pins are removed 4 weeks after the procedure. The patient is permitted to use a regular
shoe 8 to 12 weeks after the procedure. The most common complication is recurrent or
new deformity of the toes.

Metatarsal Osteotomy
Metatarsal osteotomies can be used to manage high pressure under a single ray.
High healing and low recurrence rates

Metatarsal Osteotomy
Isolated forefoot ulcers under a single metatarsal head can be managed by reducing
pressure under the metatarsal head.4 First-line management involves the use of an
accommodative insert. If shoe modifications are infective or the ulcer recurs, an
osteotomy is indicated to reduce pressure under the metatarsal head. If extensive
necrosis is present or the metatarsal is infected, resection may be a better treatment
option. An off-loading metatarsal osteotomy is associated with a 98% success rate with
regard to healing a plantar ulcer and a 3.7% complication rate.5 The high success and
low complication rate associated with the procedure makes it a reasonable approach
early in the wound care plan.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:32 AM
AAOS | Surgical Management of the Diabetic Foot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000551
10/27

Various approaches have been described. A proximal metatarsal closing wedge
osteotomy is most common. The osteotomy can be stabilized via internal fixation or with
the use of one percutaneous Kirschner wire (Figure 4). The osteotomies are healed at 6
weeks postoperatively. Patients are permitted to bear weight in off-loading shoes
immediately postoperatively.5 Minimally invasive osteotomies are associated with
minimal tissue injury and no required implants. Distal metatarsal diaphyseal osteotomy
via these techniques aid in the healing of diabetic foot ulcers.6,7
Figure 4
Lateral (A) and AP (B) radiographs of a foot demonstrate dorsiflexion osteotomy of the
first metatarsal. (Courtesy of Jerry S. Grimes, MD, Lubbock, TX.)
Partial/Complete Excision of Metatarsal Head
Partial excision of the metatarsal head usually is performed on the fifth metatarsal.
Complete excision of a single metatarsal head is tolerated with careful management of
transfer pressures postoperatively.

Partial/Complete Excision of Metatarsal Head
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:32 AM
AAOS | Surgical Management of the Diabetic Foot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000551
11/27

If extensive necrosis is present or the metatarsal head has been infected or exposed,
partial or complete excision of the metatarsal head is indicated. The risk for transfer
lesions after excision of a metatarsal head can be managed in patients who have
neuropathy and involvement of only a single metatarsal head. Careful attention to shoe
wear and foot care may prevent increased pressure on the adjacent metatarsals from
resulting in new ulcerations.4
Partial excision of the plantar metatarsal head is associated with the advantage of a
lower incidence of transfer lesion because of the continued weight bearing of the
residual metatarsal. Partial excision is easiest to perform on the fifth metatarsal head via
a lateral approach (Figure 5). A saw is used to resect the most plantar portion of the
metatarsal head. Repair of the capsule is important to prevent deformity. A stiff shoe is
used until the ulcer heals.
Figure 5
Lateral radiographs of a foot that underwent condylectomy of the fifth ray obtained
before excision (A) and after partial excision of the plantar condyle (B). (Courtesy of Jerry
S. Grimes, MD, Lubbock, TX.)
Complete excision of the metatarsal head is indicated if the soft-tissue envelope is
severely compromised. All necrotic or infected tissue should be excised. This often
requires ellipsing out the ulcer via a full-thickness incision through all the affected tissue
and may require resection to the bone. A separate dorsal incision is made over the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:32 AM
AAOS | Surgical Management of the Diabetic Foot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000551
12/27

metatarsal. Using a saw, an angled cut is made from dorsal-distal to plantar-proximal to
prevent a sharp edge in the area of soft-tissue compromise.4
Complete excision of multiple metatarsal heads has been described. Typically, this
requires removal of all the lesser metatarsal heads with or without the first metatarsal.
This technique is similar to rheumatoid foot reconstruction techniques and typically is
well tolerated. The toes are retained; however, they essentially are nonfunctional.
Achilles Tendon Lengthening
Level A evidence for Achilles tendon lengthening for the management of forefoot ulcers
Reduced recurrence of forefoot ulcers
Overlengthening may result in calcaneal ulcer.

Achilles Tendon Lengthening
For patients with forefoot ulcerations and a tight Achilles tendon on physical
examination, Achilles tendon lengthening is one of the most effective procedures.
Lengthening of Achilles tendon substantially reduces the recurrence rate of forefoot
ulcers managed via total contact cast immobilization. Level I evidence for Achilles tendon
lengthening is associated with a Grade A recommendation in multiple reviews however,
concern for complications, especially calcaneal ulcers, and extended postoperative
immobilization limit the use of the procedure.8
Achilles tendon lengthening is indicated in patients with an equinus contracture (less
than 5° of dorsiflexion) and a forefoot ulcer. The procedure typically is performed under
a regional or general anesthetic agent. The ankle is placed in maximum dorsiflexion with
the knee extended. A No. 15 blade is inserted into the midsubstance of the Achilles
tendon 2 cm above the calcaneus. The medial half of the tendon is released. The scalpel
is inserted into the midsubstance of the Achilles tendon 2 cm more proximal, and the
lateral half of the tendon is released. Next, the scalpel is inserted into the midsubstance
of the Achilles tendon 2 cm more proximal, and the medial half of the tendon is

9/4/26, 10:32 AM
AAOS | Surgical Management of the Diabetic Foot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000551
13/27

released. Because of the spiral nature of the Achilles tendon, the entire tendon does not
rupture but lengthens. Using controlled pressure, the ankle is dorsiflexed to 20° to 30°.
The leg is splinted in slight dorsiflexion. The patient does not bear weight for 6 weeks
after the procedure and is immobilized for 3 months after the procedure.
An alternative to an Achilles lengthening is a gastrocnemius recession. This can be
accomplished through an open or endoscopic procedure. This technique is less likely to
result in overlengthening compared to an Achilles lengthening.8 A 3-cm medial or
midline incision is placed at the distal palpable musculotendinous junction of the
gastrocnemius. Blunt dissection is performed through the subcutaneous tissue to the
crural fascia. Care should be taken to avoid the sural nerve. The crural fascia is divided
longitudinally. A hemostat is used to bluntly develop a plane between the gastrocnemius
tendon and the soleus muscle. The fascia of the gastrocnemius is sharply cut
transversely. The ankle is brought through range of motion with the knee fully extended
to determine if adequate dorsiflexion has been achieved. The crural fascia is closed with
the use of absorbable sutures. The leg is immobilized in neutral or slight dorsiflexion for
4 weeks postoperatively.
Resection Arthroplasty of the First Metatarsal Phalangeal Joint (Keller Procedure)
Indicated for plantar ulcers of the first toe
Transfer lesions are common.

Resection Arthroplasty of the First Metatarsal Phalangeal Joint
(Keller Procedure)
Resection of the base of the first phalanx was described to correct hallux valgus. The
procedure increases range of motion of the first metatarsophalangeal joint and reduces
pressure applied by the first toe. The procedure has been described to manage
recalcitrant ulcerations of the interphalangeal joint of the first ray.9
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:32 AM
AAOS | Surgical Management of the Diabetic Foot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000551
14/27

Resection arthroplasty of the first metatarsophalangeal joint is indicated in patients who
have undergone more than 6 months of nonsurgical treatment for a plantar ulceration
of the first toe and have limited range of motion of the joint. The first
metatarsophalangeal joint is exposed via a dorsal medial longitudinal approach. A
capsular flap is raised with the proximal edge intact. The proximal 30% of the proximal
phalanx is resected. The flap of capsule is sutured across the metatarsal head. The toe is
held in reduction with the use of a Kirschner wire (Figure 6). The incision is closed in a
layered fashion. The patient is permitted to bear weight as tolerated in a stiff surgical
shoe. The pins are removed 3 to 4 weeks postoperatively.
Figure 6
Lateral (A) and AP (B) fluoroscopic images of a foot show resection arthroplasty
metatarsal phalangeal joint. (Courtesy of Jerry S. Grimes, MD, Lubbock, TX.)
The procedure reduces pressure under the first toe, resulting in a high rate of healing of
the primary ulcer. The pressure is distributed to the adjacent metatarsal heads, which
may result in transfer lesions of the other metatarsal heads. Patients may require
custom, inlay extra-depth shoes with accommodative orthotics to decrease the risk of
new ulcers because of transferred pressure.9
Toe Amputation
First-toe amputations that retain the base of the proximal phalanx are associated with better
function.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:32 AM
AAOS | Surgical Management of the Diabetic Foot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000551
15/27

Complete amputation of the middle lesser metatarsals will cause the remaining toes to drift to
fill the gap.

Toe Amputation
Amputation of a toe is indicated if necrosis or infection compromises the digit. The level
of amputation often is driven by the remaining viable soft tissues. Typically, the bone cut
is 5 mm more proximal than the distal extent of the viable tissue. If osteomyelitis is
present, the amputation should remove all infected bone.4
First-toe amputation results in increased pressure under the first metatarsal, lesser
metatarsal heads, and remaining toes, increasing the risk of ulcers and additional
amputation. Retention of the proximal 1 cm of the proximal phalanx will maintain flexor
hallucis brevis function and prevent retraction of the sesamoid apparatus. This may help
mitigate transfer pressure.
Removal of a lesser toe results in a potential space, which the remaining toes shift to fill.
This may cause symptomatic hallux valgus. Retention of part of the proximal phalanx
may reduce the shift of adjacent digits (Figure 7). If the level of viable tissue approaches
the metatarsophalangeal joint, achieving viable margins and still having adequate soft
tissue to close the incision may be difficult. The surgeon should be prepared to extend
the procedure more proximally.10

Ray Amputation
Ray amputations remove the toe and part of the metatarsal.
Lateral ray amputations are better tolerated.
If less than two rays are removed, shoe wear is better.

Ray Amputation
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:32 AM
AAOS | Surgical Management of the Diabetic Foot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000551
17/27

Amputation of a toe and part of the metatarsal, or ray amputation, often is required to
attain adequate surgical margins for forefoot infections. Preserving the bases of the
metatarsals allows the Lisfranc joint to remain stable and should be attempted if
possible. Typically, patients tolerate partial lateral foot amputations better than partial
medial amputations. Amputation of the entire fifth metatarsal is poorly tolerated
because of the loss of the peroneal brevis to oppose the pull of the posterior tibialis.4
First ray amputations may increase load to the adjacent rays. In addition, loss of the
anterior tibialis insertion may weaken ankle dorsiflexion. In general, lateral ray
amputations are better tolerated than medial ray amputations. Amputation of one or
two rays may result in a foot that fits in a standard shoe; however, amputation of three
or more rays often results in the need for a high-top shoe to hold the shoe to the
shortened foot.
In general, ray amputations are more durable and functional than complete
transmetatarsal amputations (TMAs; Figure 8). Patients who undergo a ray amputation
have fewer problems with shoe wear and a more normal gait. Patients who undergo
complete TMA have a shortened stride. A patient with a TMA requires less energy for gait
than a patient with a transtibial amputation, and TMA leaves a patient with a distal
weight-bearing residual limb without the need for an expensive prosthesis. (Resource 3);
Video 2).

Muscle balance should be assessed to determine the need for Achilles tendon
lengthening and/or tendon transfer. Ray resection is associated with a high failure rate.
TMA is associated with a revision surgery rate as high as 82%.10
Midfoot Amputation
Amputation in the midfoot is through the Lisfranc or Chopart joints.

Midfoot Amputation
The advantages of a midfoot amputation are that it retains a functional
tibiotalar joint and the normal weight-bearing soft tissue of the heel. High
ambulatory levels have been reported in patients who undergo midfoot
amputation. The disadvantages of a midfoot amputation are a shortenedSEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:32 AM
AAOS | Surgical Management of the Diabetic Foot
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000551
19/27

anatomic lever arm, reduced push-off, difficulty with stability, and development
of equinovarus deformity. Patients who undergo midfoot amputation require a
more extensive prosthesis than patients who undergo TMA. Midfoot
amputations rarely are performed in patients with diabetes mellitus.10
Hindfoot Amputation
Hindfoot amputation retains the plantar heel soft tissue for weight bearing.
Hindfoot amputations include Syme, Pirogoff, and Boyd amputations.
Prostheses for hindfoot amputation are more difficult to fabricate than those for
transtibial amputation.

Hindfoot Amputation
The primary advantage of a hindfoot amputation over more proximal
amputations is its potential for a full–load-bearing residual limb that is nearly
normal in length and requires less energy expenditure during walking.
Candidates for hindfoot amputation are patients with good potential for
ambulation with a prosthesis postoperatively, a viable heel pad, no infection at
the heel pad level, and adequate vascularity. A Pirogoff amputation avoids the
extensive dissection about the calcaneus required by a Syme amputation but
depends on bone union. A Pirogoff amputation also results in a more stable
heel pad that is better able to withstand ambulation without a prosthesis. The
fitting of a prothesis after a hindfoot amputation may be difficult, and compared
with a transtibial amputation, less space is available for mechanical structures
to enhance the performance of the prosthesis10 (Figure 9).

postoperative splint. (Courtesy of Jerry S. Grimes, MD, Lubbock, TX.)
A Syme amputation can be performed in two stages approximately 6 weeks
apart. Most surgeons use a single-stage technique because the results are
essentially the same as those of a two-stage procedure; however, the costs and
the risk of perioperative complications are lower with only one procedure.
Successful healing is reported in 84.5% of patients who undergo single-stage
amputation. Heel pad migration after a Syme amputation is reported in as many
as 25% of patients and can be reduced by anchoring the heel pad to the distal
tibia.10,11 Wound healing is correlated with posterior tibial artery patency

Patients require ankle-foot orthosis bracing postoperatively.

Partial Calcanectomy
Patients with a recurrent heel ulcer, nonhealing heel ulcer, or osteomyelitis of
the calcaneus are candidates for a partial calcanectomy (Figure 10). Healing via
secondary intention and the use of a split-thickness skin graft to manage these
defects are not durable for long-term weight bearing. Patients with ulcers in the
posterolateral aspect of the calcaneus managed via free flaps are unable to
wear normal shoes because of widening of the heel. Before partial
calcanectomy, nutritional status should be evaluated. In addition, patients
without a palpable pulse should undergo revascularization preoperatively.13,14

The surgical incision is dictated by the shape and location of the tissue defect.
The incision should be full thickness and fully excise the lesion. The incision
includes proximal and distal extensions to allow for exposure of the Achilles
tendon and plantar fascial insertions. The Achilles tendon and the plantar fascia
are sharply released. Periosteal elevators are used to raise soft-tissue flaps on
the medial and lateral aspects of the calcaneus. A wide osteotome is used to
resect the calcaneus from just posterior to the subtalar joint to the inferior
margin of the calcaneocuboid joint. The wound is closed primarily over a drain.
The foot is splinted in plantar flexion for 6 weeks postoperatively. After the
wound heals, the patient is permitted to bear weight, and a custom ankle-foot
orthosis is used to support the soft tissues and prevent recurrent skin
breakdown. Results in the literature range from 30% to 100% healing.13-15

Postoperative Management
A multidisciplinary diabetic foot care team should be involved to minimize the likelihood
of major amputation and improve the patient’s quality of life.1 Multidisciplinary care
must include proper patient education to help patients avoid complications by
controlling their blood glucose level, blood pressure, and serum lipid level.1 The
American Diabetes Association reports that multidisciplinary foot care programs in
combination with comprehensive patient education can reduce lower extremity
amputation rates by as much as 45% to 60%.1
